title: Organizing a List
objective: Order the items in a list permanently with .sort() or temporarily with sorted(), reverse a list with .reverse(), and measure it with len().

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Python gives you two different ways to sort a list, and the difference matters. scores.sort() rearranges scores in place — the original order is gone for good. sorted(scores) instead builds and returns a brand-new sorted list while leaving scores exactly as it was, which is useful when you still need the original order later.
list_name.reverse() flips the current order of a list in place — first becomes last and last becomes first. It does not sort anything; it just reverses whatever order the items were already in.
len(list_name) returns how many items are currently in a list. It's a plain function call, not a method, so you write len(scores) rather than scores.len().
explanation.rule: sort() changes the list forever; sorted() hands you a new list and leaves the original alone; reverse() flips the current order; len() counts the items.

examples.title: Permanent vs. Temporary Order
examples.note: sorted(scores) returns a new ordered list without touching scores. Only scores.sort() changes scores itself.

examples.title: Reverse and Count
examples.note: reverse() flips the existing order in place; len() reports how many items remain.

options: scores is unchanged; sort() returns a new list
scores is now permanently rearranged in ascending order

assignment.title: Leaderboard
assignment.brief: Write show_leaderboard(scores) that prints the original scores, a temporarily sorted view, confirmation the original is untouched, the permanently sorted list, the reversed list, and the total number of entries.
requirements: Print sorted(scores) labeled "Temporary sort:" without changing scores yet.
Print scores again labeled "Still original:" to prove it hasn't changed.
Call scores.sort() and print it labeled "Permanently sorted:".
Call scores.reverse() and print it labeled "Reversed:".
assignment.starterCode:
def show_leaderboard(scores):
    # Print original, temporary sort, original again, permanent sort, reversed, and count.
    pass

show_leaderboard([42, 17, 89, 3])
assignment.solutionCode:
def show_leaderboard(scores):
    print("Original:", scores)
    print("Temporary sort:", sorted(scores))
    print("Still original:", scores)
    scores.sort()
    print("Permanently sorted:", scores)
    scores.reverse()
    print("Reversed:", scores)
    print("Total entries:", len(scores))

show_leaderboard([42, 17, 89, 3])

scores.reverse() flips whatever order scores is currently in — call it after sort() so the reversal is of the sorted order.
len(scores) goes last, after both sort() and reverse() have already run.
